column4: The dead are "رُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ" and the same ayah declares "لَهُ الْحُكْمُ"; it fuses the section's returning hand, true Master, and final Judge in one scene.
Noah appeals over his drowned son and says "أَنْتَ أَحْكَمُ الْحَاكِمِينَ"; the section's closing title becomes the language of trust when a divine decision is painful.
Shuayb tells the believing and unbelieving parties to wait until God judges between them, calling Him "خَيْرُ الْحَاكِمِينَ"; judgment restrains a conflict people cannot settle.
The Messenger is told to follow revelation and endure "حَتَّىٰ يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ" because He is the best of judges, directly matching the section's stance of waiting for God's decision.
Joseph's eldest brother refuses to leave until his father permits it or God judges for him, then says He is "خَيْرُ الْحَاكِمِينَ"; judgment is the release from a binding pledge.
The question "وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ حُكْمًا" is a near counterpart to 95:8, while its contrast with جاهلية makes God's best judgment the boundary against distorted human rule.
God will judge on the Day of Resurrection concerning the very matters people disputed, directly identifying the judge's day described in the section.
The ayah joins "لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ", "لَهُ الْحُكْمُ", and "إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ"; the worshiped one, Judge, and destination of return are explicitly one.
After forbidding invocation of another deity, the ayah says everything perishes except God, "لَهُ الْحُكْمُ", and to Him all are returned; it gathers worship, judgment, and return.
إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ is immediately joined to the command to worship none but Him, exactly supporting the section's claim that the worshiped one and the Judge are the same.
Every disputed matter has its judgment with God; the speaker then names Him as Lord, trusts Him, and turns to Him, binding adjudication to return and servitude.
The Prophet says "إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ" and that God tells the truth and is the best separator, making divine judgment an act that distinguishes truth rather than mere power.
أَفَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أَبْتَغِي حَكَمًا rejects seeking any other judge because God sent the fully explained Book; the rhetorical question places the proper answer in the hearer's mouth.
God commands trusts to be restored and commands that, when people judge, they judge with justice; this is the section's dictionary sense of restraint from wrongdoing made normative.
David is ordered to judge people in truth and not follow desire lest it divert him from God's path; just judgment functions as the rein that checks impulse.
If the Prophet judges the parties who come to him, he must judge equitably, and God loves the equitable; the ayah states the corrective justice built into the section's root account.
The Prophet must judge by what God revealed and resist desires; the ayah then makes God the common return who will disclose disputed matters.
The command to judge by revelation is coupled with warnings against desires and seduction away from God's rulings, presenting judgment as active restraint for correction.
People given scripture are called to God's Book "لِيَحْكُمَ بَيْنَهُمْ", yet a party turns away; this is the section's scene of summoning parties to divine judgment and their refusal.
Faith is denied until people make the Messenger judge their disputes, feel no inward resistance, and submit fully; accepting judgment becomes concrete willing subjection.
When they are called to God and His Messenger "لِيَحْكُمَ بَيْنَهُمْ", a party turns away, exactly staging the summons to judgment described by the section.
Believers answer the same summons to God's and the Messenger's judgment with "سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا"; judgment and obedient submission meet in the response.
Those claiming belief seek the judgment of ṭāghūt despite being commanded to reject it; the ayah exposes the rival submission implied whenever God's judgment is refused.
Once God and His Messenger decide a matter, believing men and women have no remaining choice; divine decision places desire under a binding limit.
On that Day sovereignty belongs to God and He judges between believers and unbelievers, uniting ownership, the day, and adjudication.
Those who rejected God alone but believed when partners were joined are told "فَالْحُكْمُ لِلَّهِ"; exclusive judgment answers a failure of exclusive worship.
God admits no one as a partner in His judgment, giving a direct boundary to the section's identification of the worshiped one as sole Judge.
The Lord decides Israel's disputes "بِحُكْمِهِ" and is mighty and knowing; judgment here carries the knowledge needed to hit the truth.
The prayer to Creator and Knower asks Him to judge between His servants concerning their disagreements, joining creation, knowledge, and final decision.
The Messenger prays "رَبِّ احْكُمْ بِالْحَقِّ" amid hostile descriptions, making judgment in truth the answer sought under pressure.
وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ is the section's quoted question naming the Judge's day of reckoning and recompense.
The repeated question about "يَوْمُ الدِّينِ" intensifies the inability to master that day's meaning before the following ayah supplies its decisive feature.
No soul can do anything for another on that day and "الْأَمْرُ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلَّهِ"; this is the section's answer that all command then belongs to the Judge.
مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ names the worshiped Lord as owner of the day of judgment, account, and recompense developed in the section.
وَإِنَّ الدِّينَ لَوَاقِعٌ asserts under oath that the reckoning or recompense must occur, answering the denial asked about in 95:7.
At resurrection the deniers cry "هَذَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ"; what was denied becomes a recognized scene before the Judge.
أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ بِالدِّينِ directly parallels 95:7's question about denying the reckoning and lets the following conduct expose what that denial means.
The faithful are those who affirm "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ"; their certainty is the direct counterpart to the denial challenged in 95:7.
The condemned confess "وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ", showing the final consequence of the denial questioned by the surah.
The transgressing deniers are identified as those who deny "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", a direct repetition of the section's link between denial and final judgment.
On that day God pays people "دِينَهُمُ الْحَقَّ", their full and true recompense; dīn appears as the just due administered by the Judge.

At a dying person's bedside the challengers are asked whether they are "غَيْرَ مَدِينِينَ", outside subjection or recompense; the source dictionary's dīn sense of being under mastery becomes existential.
They are challenged to return the departing soul if truthful; failure to turn it back proves the subjection named in 56:86 and points toward God's final return.
A speaker asks whether, after death and becoming dust and bones, people will be "لَمَدِينُونَ", brought to account or recompensed; the root is tied directly to resurrection.
يَوْمَ يَقُومُ النَّاسُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ is the exact standing-before-the-Lord scene used by the section to explain qiyāmah from the q-w-m root.
Faces are humbled before "الْحَيِّ الْقَيُّومِ" and the bearer of wrongdoing fails, matching the section's scene of creation standing subject before the Living, Self-Sustaining Judge.
People are warned of a day when they are returned to God, every soul is paid in full, and none is wronged; return, recompense, and restraint of injustice coincide.
All return to God; He begins and repeats creation so believers are recompensed in justice, making creation, resurrection, return, and fair judgment one argument.
Every soul tests its prior deeds and all are "رُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلَاهُمُ الْحَقِّ"; this closely repeats 6:62's return to the true Master before false supports vanish.
God created heaven and earth in truth so each soul may be recompensed for what it earned without injustice; creation is ordered toward the just settlement implied by 95:8.
الْيَوْمَ تُجْزَىٰ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ is followed by "لَا ظُلْمَ الْيَوْمَ"; the Judge's day is precisely a restraint of wrongdoing.
The earth shines, the record and witnesses are brought, and people are judged in truth without being wronged; it makes the section's root definition a full courtroom scene.
God sets just balances for the Day of Resurrection so no soul is wronged at all, even to a mustard seed; this specifies how the final judgment prevents injustice.
On that day no soul is wronged and people receive only what they did; the self-answering resurrection question of 36:81 culminates in exact recompense.
When all are gathered on the doubtless day, every soul is paid fully and none is wronged, directly describing the just decision anticipated by the section.
Each soul comes arguing for itself, is paid fully for its deeds, and is not wronged; this stages litigants before a judgment that checks injustice.
David and Solomon judge the damaged field while God witnesses their ruling; a concrete dispute makes the meaning of الحكم visible.
God gives Solomon the right understanding of that case and gives both men "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا"; it closely embodies the source dictionary's wisdom as reaching truth through knowledge and reason.
When Joseph matures, God gives him "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا"; the pairing concretely supports the section's link between judgment, wisdom, and knowledge.
At maturity Moses is likewise given "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا", repeating the union of sound judgment and knowledge behind the section's definition of wisdom.
Lot receives "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا" and is rescued from a town practicing corrupt acts, so discerning judgment is joined to deliverance from wrongdoing.
David is given wisdom and decisive speech, "الْحِكْمَةَ وَفَصْلَ الْخِطَابِ"; wisdom here equips the ruler to separate and settle claims rightly.
The covenant question "أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ" receives "بَلَىٰ"; it is the section's exact grammatical model for a negative question that demands affirmation.
The negative question asks whether the Creator of heaven and earth can create their like and answers "بَلَىٰ"; creative power places affirmation of resurrection in the listener's mouth.
فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ supplies the creating and proportioning premise which the section says leads to the final question about reviving the dead.
أَلَيْسَ ذَٰلِكَ بِقَادِرٍ matches 95:8's form exactly: a negative question makes the hearer affirm that the creator can resurrect.
When people are made to stand before their Lord, He asks "أَلَيْسَ هَذَا بِالْحَقِّ" and they answer "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّنَا"; the section's question-and-affirmation form occurs inside final judgment.
At the Fire the same question "أَلَيْسَ هَذَا بِالْحَقِّ" draws "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّنَا", showing the forced affirmation that follows earlier denial.
The human being was first a drop of emitted fluid; this is the opening bodily stage in the argument that creation entails the power to resurrect and judge.
God makes the created human into the two sexes, completing the sequence between "فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ" and the final self-answering resurrection question.
A human created from a drop becomes an open disputant; the created creature's challenge sets up the judgment-bearing question answered in 36:81.
The disputant forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones, identifying the denial that the following creator argument overturns.
The answer is that the one who originated the bones the first time will revive them and knows every creation; first creation grounds return and divine knowledge.
After the creation argument, all dominion is in God's hand and "إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ"; ability to recreate ends in return to the sovereign Judge.
A negative question asks whether the God who created the heavens and earth can revive the dead, then answers "بَلَىٰ"; it is a direct parallel to both 36:81 and 75:40.
The deniers are asked whether the Creator of heaven and earth can create their like; the self-answering creation argument leads to an appointed resurrection term.
Successive human stages and revived earth are displayed to remove doubt about resurrection, making created form evidence for the return before judgment.
The embryo passes through measured forms until God produces another creation and is praised as "أَحْسَنُ الْخَالِقِينَ"; excellent formation is the premise for what follows.
After that formation, human beings certainly die; this supplies the transition from first creation to the return discussed by the section.
After death people are raised on the Day of Resurrection, completing the creator-to-judgment logic of the closing question.
God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him; origination and return are stated as one ordered movement.
God gives life to the dead, causes death, gives life again, and to Him people are returned; the whole return-to-Judge sequence is compressed into one ayah.
God gives life, causes death, and gathers everyone on the doubtless Day of Resurrection; creation and death issue in the judicial gathering.
The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire receives the Garden; it unites the courtroom stance with the source dictionary's restraint.

Shackles rise to the deniers' chins and force their heads up; this is a Quranic physical analogue to the source dictionary's bridle-piece surrounding the jaw and preventing a creature from rushing free.
God cancels Satan's intrusion and then "يُحْكِمُ اللَّهُ آيَاتِهِ"; this h-k-m usage visibly performs the source dictionary's restraint for correction and firming.
They ask the Prophet to judge although the Torah contains "حُكْمُ اللَّهِ", then turn away; the ayah combines possession of divine judgment with refusal to submit to it.
Prophets judge by the Torah God revealed, and refusal to judge by revelation is named unbelief; transmitted law places a firm boundary on the judge.
The revealed law sets measured redress for injuries and calls those who do not judge by God's revelation wrongdoers, making judgment itself a check on ظلم.
The people of the Gospel are told to judge by what God revealed, and refusal is called defiance; divine judgment is presented as a binding corrective norm.
Believers must stand firmly for justice even against themselves or close kin and must not follow desire; self-restraint makes truthful judgment possible.
Hatred must not drive believers away from justice; the command to be just makes restraint from wrongdoing operate precisely when passion pushes hardest.
A transgressing party is resisted until it returns to God's command, after which reconciliation must be just; return, restraint, reform, and equity form one process.
God tells Jesus that all parties return to Him and He will judge their disputes; return and decision are explicitly the endpoint of their division.
Mutually condemning scriptural communities are told that God will judge their dispute on the Day of Resurrection, a direct repeated occurrence of the section's court scene.
God judges believers and hypocrites on the Day of Resurrection and denies unbelievers a final way over believers, making judgment the definitive settlement.
After the Children of Israel divide despite knowledge, their Lord will judge their disputes on the Resurrection Day; knowledge without right judgment becomes accountable.
The Lord will judge on the Day of Resurrection between those who disputed about the Sabbath, joining a concrete legal dispute to final adjudication.
God separates the named religious communities on the Day of Resurrection and witnesses everything; the Judge resolves divisions spanning whole communities.
The Lord will decide between people on the Day of Resurrection concerning their disputes; the nonlexical "يفصل" repeats judgment as separation.
Pure dīn belongs to God, false protectors claim to mediate worship, and God judges their dispute; servitude, divine ownership, and adjudication are inseparable.
People differ after knowledge through rivalry, and the Lord judges their disputes on the Resurrection Day; final judgment corrects knowledge distorted by desire.
People are told to act and are then "تُرَدُّونَ" to the Knower of unseen and seen, who informs them of their deeds; return leads directly to disclosure and account.
The death people flee will meet them, then they are "تُرَدُّونَ" to the Knower who reports their deeds; unavoidable death becomes the road back to judgment.
إِنَّ إِلَيْنَا إِيَابَهُمْ makes the people's homeward return belong to God alone, beginning a compact end-of-surah counterpart to Tīn's close.
ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا حِسَابَهُمْ makes their account God's charge, completing 88:25's return with the Judge's reckoning.
A human given scripture, judgment, and prophethood cannot tell people to worship him instead of God; possession of حكم is sharply distinguished from being the one worshiped.
The revealed restraints just listed are called part of the Lord's wisdom, and the ayah again forbids setting another deity with God; wisdom orders conduct under the worshiped one.
Jesus comes with wisdom and says he will clarify some disputed matters, linking wisdom to the accurate resolution of disagreement.
Wrongdoers suppose they will be made equal to believers in life and death, and the ayah says "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ"; bad human judgment is exposed by the just distinction of the next ayah.
The question whether the submitting are to be treated like criminals rejects an indiscriminate outcome, clarifying that just judgment must distinguish morally unlike lives.
مَا لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ challenges the hearers' warped verdict, a direct foil to the closing affirmation of God as best Judge.
Those doing evil imagine they can outrun God and are told "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ"; their judgment denies the return that divine judgment enforces.
The man ashamed of a daughter deliberates whether to keep her in humiliation or bury her, and "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ" condemns a judgment that produces the very ظلم judgment should prevent.
After contrasting God, who guides to truth, with powerless partners, the ayah asks "فَمَا لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ"; accurate judgment must follow the one who reaches and guides to truth.
Arbitrary shares are assigned to God and alleged partners, ending "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ"; invented cultic judgment reverses the section's union of worship and God's rule.
مَا لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ rebukes the claim that God has daughters; the hearers' verdict is placed under the question of the true Judge.
At death a person pleads "رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ" to return and act rightly; the desired return to earthly choice is set against the unavoidable return to judgment.
The request to return is refused and a barrier remains until resurrection; this boundary distinguishes a revoked earthly return from the final raising no one can evade.
Standing over the Fire, deniers wish they could be returned and cease denying; the scene reveals too late what the section's present question asks them to affirm now.
God says that, if returned, they would resume what was forbidden; mere reversal to earthly life would not accomplish the corrective restraint imagined by their plea.

Joseph could not have taken his brother under "دِينِ الْمَلِكِ" except by God's will; this worldly king's regime displays the source dictionary's dīn sense of governing subjection beside God's final dīn.
The curse on Iblis lasts until "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", making the day of recompense the fixed limit at which deferred judgment arrives.
Abraham hopes his Lord will forgive his fault on "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ"; the Judge's day is approached through personal hope as well as fear.
Iblis's curse is extended to "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", again marking that day as the terminus of respite and the onset of settled recompense.
The deniers' scalding hospitality is identified as their reception on "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", giving concrete consequence to the day denied in 95:7.
The wicked enter the blaze on "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ"; the named day carries enacted recompense, not an abstract calendar label.
All in heaven and earth belongs to God and "لَهُ الدِّينُ وَاصِبًا"; enduring obedience or subjection belongs to the same owner whose judgment governs the final day.
All in heaven and earth submits to God willingly or unwillingly and is returned to Him, giving a nonlexical statement of the source dictionary's dīn sense of subjection.
God gives wisdom to whom He wills, and its recipient has abundant good; the h-k-m derivative names a divinely granted capacity for right discernment.
Luqman is given wisdom and told to be grateful; wisdom reaches its right practical conclusion in recognition of the giver.
Calling to God's way requires wisdom, good instruction, and the best manner of argument; right discernment governs speech meant to correct rather than coerce.
Abraham asks God to grant him "حُكْمًا" and join him with the righteous, treating sound judgment as a gift that directs a life rightly.
Yahya is given "الْحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا"; judgment or wisdom is shown as a divine gift even before ordinary adult experience.
The Book's verses are "أُحْكِمَتْ" and then detailed by one Wise and Aware; the h-k-m root here means made firm or precise, a distinct extension of restraining disorder.
The Book contains "آيَاتٌ مُحْكَمَاتٌ" that anchor it, while crooked hearts pursue ambiguity; firmness of wording restrains interpretive deviation.
Noah's son trusts a mountain to save him, but the wave separates them and he is drowned; this is the anguish within which 11:45 names God best Judge.
The flood is commanded to subside and "قُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ"; the settled decree immediately precedes Noah's appeal to the best of judges.
God rules that Noah's son is not of his true family because his conduct is unrighteous and warns Noah against asking without knowledge; divine judgment corrects kinship-based expectation.
Noah seeks refuge and forgiveness after the correction, showing submission to the judgment he had invoked in 11:45.
Shuayb prays for God to decide between his people and the believers in truth, calling Him the best opener; a different verb voices the same entrusting of conflict to God.
Noah asks God to decide between him and his denying people and save the believers, a non-h-k-m formulation of judgment sought in distress.
Disputes are to be referred to God and the Messenger, supplying the practical act behind the section's phrase about calling parties to God's judgment.
When hypocrites are told to come to what God revealed and to the Messenger, they turn away emphatically, continuing 4:60's rejected summons to judgment.
The Book is sent in truth so the Prophet may judge people by what God has shown him, while he is forbidden to advocate for betrayers; revelation reins in partiality.
God sends scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their disputes, locating sound adjudication in revealed guidance.
Jacob takes precautions yet says "إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ" and trusts Him, distinguishing prudent action from possession of the final decision.
Rules governing believing migrant women are called "حُكْمُ اللَّهِ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ", showing divine judgment ordering a difficult human separation.
Those offering excuses are told they will be returned to the Knower of unseen and seen, who will report their deeds; concealed motives cannot evade the returning Judge.
The soul reaches the throat while those present watch; this bedside scene makes the challenge about being unsubjected and returning it in 56:86-87 concrete.
إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمَسَاقُ makes the dying person's drive end at the Lord, linking the same surah's creation argument to final return.
At Hell's gates the keepers ask whether messengers came, and the condemned answer "بَلَىٰ"; a negative question draws the admission that seals judgment.
Hell's keepers ask "أَوَلَمْ تَكُ تَأْتِيكُمْ رُسُلُكُمْ" and the sufferers answer "بَلَىٰ"; the forced yes acknowledges the evidence behind the sentence.
Each cast group is asked by Hell's keepers "أَلَمْ يَأْتِكُمْ نَذِيرٌ"; the negative question prepares the explicit affirmation in the next ayah.
The group answers "بَلَىٰ قَدْ جَاءَنَا نَذِيرٌ" and admits denial; the section's grammar becomes a confession at judgment.
Hypocrites ask believers "أَلَمْ نَكُنْ مَعَكُمْ" and receive "بَلَىٰ", but a barrier now separates them; verbal affirmation cannot erase the earlier choices under judgment.
God asks Abraham "أَوَلَمْ تُؤْمِنْ" and he answers "بَلَىٰ" before the demonstration of reviving birds; the same grammar joins affirmation to confidence in resurrection.
أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِكَافٍ عَبْدَهُ uses the same self-answering negative form to make God's sufficiency for His servant something the hearer must affirm.
أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِعَزِيزٍ ذِي انْتِقَامٍ uses the same form to compel acknowledgment of the power that enforces judgment.
With collars on their necks and chains, the condemned are dragged away; it extends the source dictionary's physical restraint image from a guiding bridle to punitive restraint.
The one God is named "الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ", matching the divine title before whom the section's dictionary account says creation stands on the Resurrection Day.
لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ joins the sole worshiped God to the Living, Self-Sustaining name used in the section's standing scene.
Abraham asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, and believers "يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الْحِسَابُ"; the account itself is pictured as standing or being established.
God promises to aid His messengers and believers "يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الْأَشْهَادُ"; witnesses standing turns the final judgment into a courtroom event.
God commands justice and beneficence and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and transgression; divine command performs the corrective prevention from ظلم in the source dictionary.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good, supplying a concise measure of the justice attributed to the best Judge.
Good is repaid tenfold while evil receives only its equivalent and none are wronged; recompense is both measured and merciful.
When every wrongdoer sees the punishment, judgment is made in equity and no one is wronged, continuing the section's court meaning without the h-k-m root.
The record is set down, deeds are found present, and "لَا يَظْلِمُ رَبُّكَ أَحَدًا"; documentary account displays how the Judge prevents injustice.
Each person has ranks according to deeds so God may pay them fully without injustice; differentiated recompense embodies accurate judgment.
God owns heaven and earth so that evil is recompensed by deeds and excellence rewarded with the best; ownership serves discriminating judgment.
God judges and no one can reverse or review His judgment, then the ayah names Him swift in account; the Judge's decision is both final and answerable to no higher court.
The Prophet says the Lord will gather the two sides and decide between them in truth, calling Him the knowing Decider; gathering, knowledge, and just settlement meet in one answer.
During the inhabitants of the Fire's dispute, the arrogant say that God has already judged between the servants; the verdict has become an irreversible condition shared by both parties.
God decides in truth, while the beings invoked besides Him cannot decide anything; sole worship and sole effective judgment are distinguished from powerless rivals.
When God's command comes, the matter is decided in truth and falsifiers lose; the arrival of judgment turns contested claims into a settled outcome.
Every community has a messenger, and when its messenger comes the people are judged equitably without injustice; witness, decision, and the prevention of ظلم form one scene.
A marital breach calls for an arbiter from each family, and sincere desire for reconciliation receives God's aid; human حكم is explicitly a restraint exercised for إصلاح.
Compensation for deliberately hunted game is assessed by two just persons; judgment measures a corrective due rather than giving appetite free rein.

People are forbidden to pass wealth to rulers or judges in order to consume others' property sinfully; corrupted judgment produces the injustice that the section's root account says حكم should prevent.
Two litigants ask David to judge between them in truth, without exceeding justice, and to guide them to an even path; the parties themselves state the proper work of a judge.
